title: The Lift: A Nucleus on a Timetable

scenes.tts: Why would a cell copy its DNA in one place, and divide in another?
scenes.visual: Title card fades. Question on screen over the cortical wall.
scenes.narration: Why would a cell copy its DNA in one place, and divide in another?

scenes.tts: Nineteenth-century anatomists saw nuclei at many heights. They read the wall as several kinds of cells.
scenes.visual: A fixed section: nuclei at every height. Old-style labels sort them into different cell types.
scenes.narration: Nineteenth-century anatomists saw nuclei at many heights. They read the wall as several kinds of cells.

scenes.tts: In nineteen thirty-five, F. C. Sauer argued for a simpler picture. One kind of long cell, whose nucleus moves inside it.
scenes.caption: In 1935, F. C. Sauer argued for a simpler picture. One kind of long cell, whose nucleus moves inside it.
scenes.visual: The labels dissolve. Long cell outlines appear around the nuclei, one nucleus per cell. Tag: Sauer, 1935.
scenes.narration: In 1935, F. C. Sauer argued for a simpler picture. One kind of long cell, whose nucleus moves inside it.

scenes.tts: A single layer of cells with nuclei at many heights is called a pseudostratified epithelium.
scenes.visual: Label: pseudostratified epithelium = one layer, nuclei at many heights.
scenes.narration: A single layer of cells with nuclei at many heights is called a pseudostratified epithelium.

scenes.tts: Picture a lift, with the ventricle at the bottom. The shaft is the cell. The car is the nucleus.
scenes.visual: One cell becomes a lift shaft; its nucleus becomes the car. Ventricle at the ground floor.
scenes.narration: Picture a lift, with the ventricle at the bottom. The shaft is the cell. The car is the nucleus.

scenes.tts: The shaft runs all the way up to the pia. But the car only serves the lowest floors, the ventricular zone.
scenes.visual: The shaft extends to the pia. The floors inside the VZ are lit; the floors above are dim.
scenes.narration: The shaft runs all the way up to the pia. But the car only serves the lowest floors, the ventricular zone.

scenes.tts: In G one, the car rides up. It stops near the top of the ventricular zone for S phase, when DNA is copied.
scenes.caption: In G1, the car rides up. It stops near the top of the ventricular zone for S phase, when DNA is copied.
scenes.visual: The car rises (label G1) and stops near the top of the VZ, glowing (label S phase, DNA copied).
scenes.narration: In G1, the car rides up. It stops near the top of the ventricular zone for S phase, when DNA is copied.

scenes.tts: In G two, it comes back down to the ground floor, the apical surface. The cell divides there.
scenes.caption: In G2, it comes back down to the ground floor, the apical surface. The cell divides there.
scenes.visual: The car descends (label G2) to the apical surface, rounds up and splits (label M).
scenes.narration: In G2, it comes back down to the ground floor, the apical surface. The cell divides there.

scenes.tts: Each cell's car runs on its own timetable. That is why nuclei sit at every height.
scenes.visual: Zoom out: many shafts side by side, each car at a different height, all moving out of step.
scenes.narration: Each cell's car runs on its own timetable. That is why nuclei sit at every height.

scenes.tts: This movement is called interkinetic nuclear migration. Movement between divisions.
scenes.visual: Label across the bottom: interkinetic nuclear migration.
scenes.narration: This movement is called interkinetic nuclear migration. Movement between divisions.

scenes.tts: A pulse label made Sauer's cycle a timetable. Tritiated thymidine, a radioactive DNA building block, is taken up only in S phase.
scenes.visual: A still section gains a clock icon. Labelled dots enter only the nuclei near the top of the VZ.
scenes.narration: A pulse label made Sauer's cycle a timetable. Tritiated thymidine, a radioactive DNA building block, is taken up only in S phase.

scenes.tts: Give a brief pulse, then fix the tissue at intervals. Soon after the pulse, where are the labeled nuclei? And when do labeled mitoses appear?
scenes.visual: Two empty panels labelled soon after and later. A question mark over the ventricle.
scenes.narration: Give a brief pulse, then fix the tissue at intervals. Soon after the pulse, where are the labeled nuclei? And when do labeled mitoses appear?

scenes.tts: Soon after the pulse, labeled nuclei sit out in the ventricular zone. No cell in mitosis is labeled.
scenes.visual: Panel 1 fills: labelled nuclei high in the VZ; mitoses at the ventricle unlabelled.
scenes.narration: Soon after the pulse, labeled nuclei sit out in the ventricular zone. No cell in mitosis is labeled.

scenes.tts: Later, the labeled nuclei come down and divide at the ventricle.
scenes.visual: Panel 2 fills: labelled nuclei now round and dividing at the ventricle.
scenes.narration: Later, the labeled nuclei come down and divide at the ventricle.

scenes.tts: In nineteen fifty-nine, two groups reported this. Labeled nuclei moved in step with the cell cycle.
scenes.caption: In 1959, two groups reported this. Labeled nuclei moved in step with the cell cycle.
scenes.visual: Tag: Sauer and Walker; Sidman, Miale and Feder, 1959.
scenes.narration: In 1959, two groups reported this. Labeled nuclei moved in step with the cell cycle.

scenes.tts: In eleven-day mouse embryos, no labeled mitosis appeared until an hour after the injection. That lag roughly spans G two, which includes the trip back down.
scenes.caption: In eleven-day mouse embryos, no labeled mitosis appeared until an hour after the injection. That lag roughly spans G2, which includes the trip back down.
scenes.visual: A timeline: injection, then one hour with no labelled mitosis, then labelled mitoses. The gap is labelled lag to first labelled mitosis (roughly G2).
scenes.narration: In eleven-day mouse embryos, no labeled mitosis appeared until an hour after the injection. That lag roughly spans G2, which includes the trip back down.

scenes.tts: So why divide at the ventricle? The answer is partly settled.
scenes.visual: Card: why divide at the ventricle? Three rows appear: partly known, proposal, proposal.
scenes.narration: So why divide at the ventricle? The answer is partly settled.

scenes.tts: The best-supported part. For much of interphase, the centrosome sits at the apical surface, at the base of the primary cilium.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the apical foot: a centrosome at the surface, a primary cilium poking into the ventricle. Row 1: partly known.
scenes.narration: The best-supported part. For much of interphase, the centrosome sits at the apical surface, at the base of the primary cilium.

scenes.tts: A dividing cell builds its spindle from its centrosomes. On the usual account, the nucleus travels to meet them. Late in G two, the centrosome can also move to meet the nucleus.
scenes.visual: The nucleus descends while the centrosome drops a short way to meet it, just short of the surface; a spindle forms and the cell divides. Row 1 tag: usual account, not settled.
scenes.narration: A dividing cell builds its spindle from its centrosomes. On the usual account, the nucleus travels to meet them. Late in G2, the centrosome can also move to meet the nucleus.
scenes.caption: A dividing cell builds its spindle from its centrosomes. On the usual account, the nucleus travels to meet them. Late in G2, the centrosome can also move to meet the nucleus.

scenes.tts: One proposal is packing. Only a cell in mitosis is round and wide. The rest can stay thin at the surface.
scenes.visual: Top-down view of the ventricular surface: many small apical feet and a few large round mitotic cells. Row 2: proposal.
scenes.narration: One proposal is packing. Only a cell in mitosis is round and wide. The rest can stay thin at the surface.

scenes.tts: A round cell takes about twenty times the room of a thin foot. So on average, each cell needs about a tenth of a dividing cell's room.
scenes.visual: On screen, marked illustrative: 12 h cycle, 0.5 h mitosis, cells spread evenly through the cycle, so 1 cell in 24 dividing. Round cell 10 µm across: π × 5² ≈ 80 µm². Apical foot 2 × 2 µm = 4 µm², so about 20 times smaller. Average (80 + 23 × 4) / 24 ≈ 7 µm² per cell, about a tenth.
scenes.narration: A round cell takes about twenty times the room of a thin foot. So on average, each cell needs about a tenth of a dividing cell's room.

scenes.tts: Staggered timetables let more progenitors share the ventricle.
scenes.visual: The surface fills with more feet; round cells come and go in turn.
scenes.narration: Staggered timetables let more progenitors share the ventricle.

scenes.tts: A second proposal is signals. In zebrafish retina, Notch signalling was reported to fall from apical to basal. So how far a nucleus travels could change the signal it meets.
scenes.visual: A shading gradient labelled Notch signal, strong at the apical side, fading basally; two nuclei travel different distances through it and glow differently. Row 3: proposal. Tag: zebrafish retina, 2008.
scenes.narration: A second proposal is signals. In zebrafish retina, Notch signalling was reported to fall from apical to basal. So how far a nucleus travels could change the signal it meets.

scenes.tts: Now the payoff. Apical radial glia divide at the surface. So where a cell divides is a first clue to what kind it is.
scenes.visual: Payoff card: where a cell divides is a first clue to the progenitor.
scenes.narration: Now the payoff. Apical radial glia divide at the surface. So where a cell divides is a first clue to what kind it is.

scenes.tts: Most mitoses at the ventricle are apical radial glia, though some intermediate progenitors divide there too. Mitoses away from it are mostly intermediate progenitors, or outer radial glia.
scenes.visual: Several dividing cells at the ventricle (mostly apical radial glia, one tagged intermediate progenitor); others higher, away from it (intermediate progenitor or outer radial glia).
scenes.narration: Most mitoses at the ventricle are apical radial glia, though some intermediate progenitors divide there too. Mitoses away from it are mostly intermediate progenitors, or outer radial glia.

scenes.tts: To name the cell, add its shape and markers. To learn what its daughters become, you need lineage, the descendants of one cell.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: position is a clue; shape and markers name the cell; lineage names the daughters.
scenes.narration: To name the cell, add its shape and markers. To learn what its daughters become, you need lineage, the descendants of one cell.
